newsitem.title: USA: Inflammation found to play role in heart attacks.
newsitem.headline: Inflammation found to play role in heart attacks.

text.p: A study in Thursday's New England Journal of Medicine has uncovered a link between inflammation and the risk of eventually developing a heart attack or stroke.

The findings also suggest that the inflammation-fighting properties of aspirin may explain why the pain killer seems to prevent heart attacks. Until now, researchers thought that aspirin's clot-preventing properties explained its ability to prevent diseases of the heart.

Previous laboratory studies have suggested that some type of inflammation may play a role in narrowing the vital arteries of the heart. Past research has also sparked the suspicion that drugs that prevent inflammation may help reduce the risks.

Knowing that they could gauge inflammation in the body by measuring blood levels of a substance known as plasma C-reactive protein, a team of researchers led by Dr. Paul M. Ridker of Brigham and Women's Hospital in Boston tested the blood of 543 doctors who had agreed to participate in the Physicians' Health Study back in 1982.
As part of that study, some of the doctors regularly took an aspirin every other day. The rest took a placebo.

When the researchers lumped the C-reactive protein test results into four groups, they discovered that the doctors with the highest levels of C-reactive protein were three times more likely to eventually have a heart attack and twice as likely to have a stroke as the doctors with the lowest levels of the telltale protein.
C-reactive protein concentrations "can predict the risk of first myocardial infarction (heart attack) and ischemic stroke," the Ridker group concluded.
The researchers also found that the benefits of taking aspirin were greatest in the group of doctors with the highest levels of inflammation.
For doctors with virtually no inflammation, aspirin had no protective effect.
"These data suggest that inflammatory markers such as C-reactive protein may provide a method of identifying people for whom aspirin is likely to be more or less effective," the team said.
However, they emphasised that that idea needed to be tested in an experiment.

In an editorial in the Journal, Dr. Attilio Maseri of the Catholic University of the Sacred Heart in Rome said the Ridker study provided "convincing evidence" that the protein test could predict future heart attacks and strokes.

But Maseri said the test was not perfect. The levels of C-reactive protein were normal in 40 percent of patients destined to develop heart problems and they "may remain elevated for years in patients who never have" a heart attack or stroke.
